t: Why Perspective uses its own data connection
x: Why Perspective uses its own data connection Perspective is a columnar analytics engine, not a conventional DOM table. Its websocket protocol moves table updates into a browser worker and supports views, aggregations, and incremental computation without serializing the full dataset through the component tree. spaday-perspective therefore separates two kinds of state: bulk rows travel through Perspective’s native websocket; connection URL, theme, and saved workspace layout remain ordinary serializable component properties. This boundary keeps Python authoring declarative while preserving Perspective’s high-performance data path. A spaday store or transports model can still carry compact application state, such as the selected layout preset or summary metrics. Sending every row through spaday would duplicate storage and serialization work before Perspective could process the same data again. Keeping the native connection also means existing Perspective server code can be used unchanged. The wrapper only adapts lifecycle, theme, and workspace configuration to spaday. x: Use showTable to select a table’s detail panel and update filters in one action: from spaday import Invoke, by_id, element element("button").text("Buy trades").on( "click", Invoke( by_id("workspace"), "showTable", "trades", {"filter": [["side", "==", "Buy"]]}, result="shown", ), ) Declare trades in config.panel_defaults or config.tables. If only a master panel shows the table, this opens a separate detail panel using the panel defaults. Existing filters on other columns remain; the action replaces only the side clauses. The result field contains the selected panel ID for later restorePanel or export actions.

x: Keep the table returned by client.table(), then update it whenever application data changes: trades = client.table(schema, limit=1_000, name="trades") trades.update( [ { "symbol": "NVDA", "quantity": 50, "price": 182.40, } ] ) Connected viewers receive the update through Perspective’s websocket. Do not copy bulk rows into a spaday store.

t: How to stream data and change layouts
s: Add a delete button to each row
x: Create the source table with a unique index, set a command schema from a page script, and handle perspective-command in Python. The schema is a function, so Python cannot author it: from spaday import CallEndpoint, event_prop, obj from spaday.backends.starlette import serve from spaday_perspective import PerspectiveViewer, package orders = client.table(rows, name="orders", index="id") panel = PerspectiveViewer(id="orders", config=config).on( "perspective-command", CallEndpoint("POST", "/orders/delete", obj({"id": event_prop("detail.context.hit.id")}), result="reply"), ) commands = """ <script type="module"> const commands = [{ kind: "Command", key: "delete", label: "", icon: "delete", title: "Delete order" }]; const schema = ({ table, hit }) => ({ commands: table === "orders" && hit?.id?.length && !hit.row_path.length ? commands : [], }); await customElements.whenDefined("perspective-panel"); let panel; while (!(panel = document.querySelector("#orders"))) await new Promise(requestAnimationFrame); await panel.setCommandSchema(schema, { scopes: ["datagrid-row"] }); </script> """ app = serve(panel, packages=[package], head=commands) The Datagrid draws the button in its command column

x: Configure the viewer’s embedded agent once, then send prompts from your own controls. Point url at a same-origin endpoint that forwards OpenAI-style chat completions and adds the API key on the server, so the key never reaches the page: from spaday import CallEndpoint, Invoke, Sequence, SetField, by_id, element, event_prop, field, obj DOCS = "/components/perspective/vendor/@perspective-dev/viewer/dist/docs/perspective-docs.json" configure = Sequence( CallEndpoint("GET", DOCS, result="agent_docs"), Invoke( by_id("workspace"), "agentConfig", obj({"url": "/api/llm/chat/completions", "model": "claude-opus-5", "docs": field("agent_docs.body")}), ), ) ask = Invoke(by_id("workspace"), "agentPrompt", field("prompt"), result="answer") reset = Invoke(by_id("workspace"), "agentReset") panel.on("perspective-agent-tool", SetField("last_tool", event_prop("detail"))) element("button").text("Ask").on("click", ask) Run configure from a button or a spaday initial effect before the first prompt. answer holds the agent’s reply, and last_tool the JSON string of the latest tool call. See Methods for what Python cannot pass.

x: Build two workspace layouts and compute config from a small reactive field: from spaday import SetField, cond, element, eq, field, obj from spaday_perspective import PerspectiveViewer panel = PerspectiveViewer().compute( "config", obj( { "ws_url": "/perspective", "tables": ["trades"], "workspace": cond( eq(field("view"), "grouped"), grouped_layout, blotter_layout, ), } ), ) controls = element( "nav", element("button").text("Blotter").on("click", SetField("view", "blotter")), element("button").text("By symbol").on("click", SetField("view", "grouped")), ) Pass store={"view": "blotter"} to serve(). Changing the field restores only the new layout; it does not reconnect the table websocket.

t: How to stream data and change layouts
x: Perspective uses its own theme names. Compute the wrapper property explicitly: from spaday import cond, field panel.compute("theme", cond(field("dark"), "dark", "light")) The aliases map to Pro Dark and Pro Light (spaday_perspective.THEMES). A full Perspective theme name is also accepted, so to use themes of your own, put their CSS on the page and compute their names instead: panel.compute("theme", cond(field("dark"), "Acme Dark", "Acme Light"))

x: Enable region selection and cell-aligned scrolling from Python: from spaday_perspective import EditMode, PerspectiveViewer, Theme panel = PerspectiveViewer( theme=Theme.DARK, config={ "ws_url": "/perspective", "workspace": { "layout": {"type": "tab-layout", "tabs": ["trades"]}, "panels": { "trades": { "table": "trades", "plugin": "Datagrid", "plugin_config": {"edit_mode": EditMode.SELECT_REGION, "scroll_lock": True}, }, }, }, }, ) Select cells and press Ctrl+C / Cmd+C to copy them as CSV. A button outside the grid copies the same selection with Invoke(by_id("workspace"), "copy", {"method": "csv-selected"}), and the whole view with copy and no options; see Methods.

x: perspective-config-update re-dispatches whenever the user edits the workspace — drags a panel, changes a view, filters. Save the whole workspace before sending it to your endpoint: from spaday import CallEndpoint, Invoke, Sequence, by_id, field panel.on( "perspective-config-update", Sequence( Invoke(by_id("workspace"), "saveWorkspace", result="saved_workspace"), CallEndpoint("POST", "/api/layout", field("saved_workspace")), ), ) Give the wrapper id="workspace". Serve the stored token back through config["workspace"] on the next load.

t: How to stream data and change layouts
s: Mirror a table into a local worker
x: For tables that are read-heavy in the browser, mirror them client-side with a per-table architecture — reads (scrolls, sorts, filters) stop round-tripping to Python: panel = PerspectiveViewer( config={ "ws_url": "/perspective", "tables": [ {"name": "trades", "architecture": "client-server", "index": "symbol"}, "orders", # plain entries stay on the server ], "workspace": layout, } ) Omit index and limit to inherit the source table’s options, or specify them for the local copy. A local limit is ignored with a warning when the source table is indexed. Use default_architecture to set the architecture for plain table-name entries. Perspective creates the local table from a source view and maintains the replica as rows change, including deletions, clear, and replace operations. Choose the default server architecture when the table should remain on the server rather than occupy browser memory.

t: How to stream data and change layouts
s: Share Perspective with your own library
x: Perspective registers global custom element names, so a second copy on the page throws from customElements.define. If your library uses Perspective, import it by its bare specifiers and leave those imports out of your bundle: // esbuild await esbuild.build({ entryPoints: ["src/index.js"], bundle: true, format: "esm", external: [ "@perspective-dev/client", "@perspective-dev/viewer", "@perspective-dev/viewer-charts", "@perspective-dev/viewer-datagrid", ], }); Serve your bundle as a module next to packages=["perspective"]; the page’s import map resolves those imports to the copy this package already loaded. Import @perspective-dev/viewer dynamically — import("@perspective-dev/viewer") — rather than statically: it instantiates its WASM with a top-level await, so a static import holds back your whole module, and any element it defines, until the binary has loaded, and spaday can mount the page before your element exists. To share the engine itself rather than just the modules, borrow it: globalThis.__spadayPerspective.client(url) returns the websocket client the panels use for that server, and .worker() the shared local engine.

A table holds data. A view defines a query over a table. A panel displays a view in a workspace. A workspace contains the layout tree and panel configurations. The following legacy names remain supported: Canonical name Compatibility name PerspectiveViewer PerspectivePanel config.workspace config.layout config.panel_defaults config.channels config.restore_selected_tabs_only config.single_tab openTablePanel(name) openChannel(name) closeTablePanels(name) closeChannel(name) saveWorkspace() save() savePortableWorkspace() saveClean() Supplying both config names requires structurally equal values; conflicting values raise an error. The config getter preserves the supplied keys. Workspace JSON strings are accepted; when supplying both workspace aliases, their values must use the same representation. Canonical save methods write the wrapper extension retained_panel_configs_by_table. Legacy save methods keep writing closed_channels; restores accept either key and reject conflicting mappings. Both mappings store one last panel configuration per table, only for tables without open panels. The wrapper removes this metadata before calling native restoreWorkspace(). The public spaday_perspective.PerspectiveViewer validates literal configuration when serialized with to_node() (including through serve() or a widget). This includes .prop("config", ...) updates. validate_config(config) performs the same check explicitly and raises ValueError with a path such as config.layout or config.panel_defaults.trades. Browser property setters validate reactive config updates before accepting them. Computed expressions are checked when their result reaches the browser, not while authoring the expression. The wrapper checks its own settings: flags, table descriptors, and the aliases. Perspective’s migrate checks the layout and each configured panel (panel_defaults, retained configurations) against its schema ahead of time, naming the offending value by JSON pointer, such as config.layout: migrated config is invalid at `/panels/grid`: …. Information a layout upgrade would drop is rejected the same way. Plugin settings, theme names, and table and column names are the viewer’s to check when the layout is applied; it reports through perspective-error, for example Invalid `plugin_config.edit_mode`: …. The Python enums below are checked against the installed Datagri

A server table (the default) reads over the websocket: every scroll, sort, and filter round-trips to the Python server. A client-server table mirrors into a local Web Worker engine: the wrapper opens a view of the server table and passes it to the worker’s table(view, options) API. The worker client loads before the websocket client so the local copy wins the viewer’s table-name lookup. Reads are then local; the server stays authoritative for writes. Set architectures in the initial config — changing the mirrored set later reconnects. Perspective’s native mirroring maintains the replica through source updates, removals, clear, and replace operations. Wrappers using the same connection, table, and mirror options share a local table and subscription. The server architecture keeps the data on the server; a client-server mirror stores a copy in browser memory.

setCommandSchema(schema, options?) is the viewer’s own method, passed through unchanged. schema is a synchronous function from Perspective’s command context to {commands}, or null to remove it; options.scopes lists the surfaces it is evaluated for: context-menu (the default), datagrid-row, datagrid-cell and chart-tooltip. Called before the panel is connected, the schema is held and set ahead of the first workspace restore. See Perspective’s custom commands guide for the context, hit and CommandSpec. The schema is a function, so it is set from a script on the page; Python cannot author it. Python handles the result: <script type="module"> const commands = [{ kind: "Command", key: "delete", label: "", icon: "delete", title: "Delete order" }]; // a grouped row's `id` is its group path and the total row's is empty; neither is an order const schema = ({ table, hit }) => ({ commands: table === "orders" && hit?.id?.length && !hit.row_path.length ? commands : [], }); await customElements.whenDefined("perspective-panel"); let panel; while (!(panel = document.querySelector("#orders"))) await new Promise(requestAnimationFrame); await panel.setCommandSchema(schema, { scopes: ["datagrid-row"] }

The viewer’s observational events reach the panel as bubbling DOM events usable from spaday’s .on(...); the panel re-dispatches the ones Perspective does not bubble itself: perspective-click, perspective-select, perspective-global-filter, perspective-global-filter-update, perspective-config-update, perspective-toggle-settings, perspective-statusbar-pointerdown, perspective-table-delete, perspective-active-panel-update, perspective-command, and perspective-agent-tool. perspective-config-update fires on user edits (layout drags, view changes, filters). A handler can call saveWorkspace() to capture the whole workspace for persistence; the event payload is not a workspace token. Two wrapper lifecycle events complete the picture: perspective-ready fires once, after the panel has connected, loaded its tables, and applied and rendered its initial workspace config — the signal to dismiss a branded startup overlay — and perspective-error fires when a config apply fails (connection, mirror, or restore), with the error in detail, so a host can swap its loader for an error state. The cancelable *-before events are not re-dispatched; attach to the viewer directly for those.

copy(options?) and export(options?) are the viewer’s own methods, passed through unchanged. options is Perspective’s ExportOptions, {method?, panel?}: method is an ExportMethod (csv by default; csv-selected, json, json-selected, arrow, plugin, …) and panel defaults to the active panel. export resolves to the data in that method’s type, a string for the CSV methods and an object of columns for the JSON ones; it is what the example’s Export CSV button downloads. copy writes the data to the clipboard from within a user gesture, so call it directly from a click handler. It rejects when the write fails or is denied, and a -selected method rejects with “Nothing is selected” when the panel has no selection. Copying needs a secure context (HTTPS or localhost); there is no fallback. Two button patterns follow. A whole-view button calls copy() and is always enabled. A selected-view button calls copy({"method": "csv-selected"}) and is disabled until perspective-select reports a non-null detail, re-reading viewer.getSelection() when perspective-active-panel-update fires, since both address the active panel. A copy snapshots the selection when called, so later selection, focus or config changes

Perspective themes itself by name; spaday_perspective.THEMES maps page modes to those names: {"light": "Pro Light", "dark": "Pro Dark"}, the Perspective theme a panel applies for each page mode. A panel with no theme follows the nearest wa-dark / wa-light ancestor to one of these. theme and themes accept the keys as shorthands and pass any other name to Perspective unchanged, so a theme an application registers is selected by its name.

spaday_perspective.package is named perspective. Its browser asset defines <perspective-panel> and the Perspective themes, and loads Perspective’s own client, viewer, datagrid and charts modules, which the package serves under vendor/ beside their WASM binaries. Its components collection contains PerspectiveViewer; catalog returns the wrapper’s property, event, and slot schema. package.imports publishes those modules under Perspective’s bare specifiers, which spaday emits as the page’s import map: Specifier Served from @perspective-dev/client vendor/@perspective-dev/client/dist/cdn/perspective.js @perspective-dev/viewer vendor/@perspective-dev/viewer/dist/cdn/perspective-viewer.js @perspective-dev/viewer-charts vendor/@perspective-dev/viewer-charts/dist/cdn/perspective-viewer-charts.js @perspective-dev/viewer-datagrid vendor/@perspective-dev/viewer-datagrid/dist/cdn/perspective-viewer-datagrid.js Any other module on the page that imports them gets the same copy.

Config updates skip superseded work that has not started. An already-running upstream restore finishes before the newest config applies. Imperative methods remain queued in order. Saved workspaces with the same panel IDs, tables, plugins, and style settings reuse existing plugins, including inactive tabs. Only panels whose view configuration changed are restored; unchanged panels receive no per-panel restore. Comparison uses live state, so restoring a saved workspace resets user edits. Reuse requires complete saved configurations and unchanged derived tables. Incomplete configurations, added or removed panels, and table/plugin/style changes use a full restore. Perspective merges plugin and column styles during per-panel updates; full restoration preserves the replacement semantics of saved workspaces in those cases. js/tests/workspace-restores.spec.js measures layout-only changes on 48 panels and changed saved workspaces on 48 Datagrid panels over 100,000 synthetic trade rows. The larger fixture has four visible stacks, inactive tabs, grouping, sorting, and filters. It compares a full restore with changes to four existing panels and checks that the saved results match. Build a live market workspace In this tutorial, you will serve a named Perspective table and display it in a spaday component tree. Install the packages pip install "spaday[examples]" spaday-perspective "perspective-python>=4.5,<4.6" Create the server and table Save this as market_app.py: import perspective import uvicorn from perspective.handlers.starlette import PerspectiveStarletteHandler from spaday.backends.starlette import serve from spaday_perspective import PerspectiveViewer from starlette.routing import WebSocketRoute from starlette.websockets import WebSocket server = perspective.Server() client = server.new_local_client() client.table( [ {"symbol": "AAPL", "quantity": 100, "price": 211.10}, {"symbol": "MSFT", "quantity": 75, "price": 503.02}, ], name="trades", ) async def perspective_socket(websocket: WebSocket) -> None: await PerspectiveStarletteHandler( perspective_server=server, websocket=websocket, ).run() Perspective owns this websocket and the bulk table data carried by it. Add the panel Continue in the same file: # Perspective's whole-element config: a regular-layout tree plus per-panel viewer configs layout = { "layout": {"type": "tab-layout", "tabs": ["market"]}
pip install "spaday[examples]" spaday-perspective "perspective-python>=4.5,<4.6"

Save this as market_app.py: import perspective import uvicorn from perspective.handlers.starlette import PerspectiveStarletteHandler from spaday.backends.starlette import serve from spaday_perspective import PerspectiveViewer from starlette.routing import WebSocketRoute from starlette.websockets import WebSocket server = perspective.Server() client = server.new_local_client() client.table( [ {"symbol": "AAPL", "quantity": 100, "price": 211.10}, {"symbol": "MSFT", "quantity": 75, "price": 503.02}, ], name="trades", ) async def perspective_socket(websocket: WebSocket) -> None: await PerspectiveStarletteHandler( perspective_server=server, websocket=websocket, ).run() Perspective owns this websocket and the bulk table data carried by it.

Continue in the same file: # Perspective's whole-element config: a regular-layout tree plus per-panel viewer configs layout = { "layout": {"type": "tab-layout", "tabs": ["market"]}, "panels": { "market": { "table": "trades", "plugin": "Datagrid", "columns": ["symbol", "quantity", "price"], } }, } panel = PerspectiveViewer( config={ "ws_url": "/perspective", "tables": ["trades"], "workspace": layout, }, theme="light", style="height: 32rem", ) app = serve( panel, packages=["perspective"], routes=[WebSocketRoute("/perspective", perspective_socket)], ) if __name__ == "__main__": uvicorn.run(app, host="127.0.0.1", port=8000) Run python market_app.py, then open http://127.0.0.1:8000. You should see both rows in a Perspective datagrid. You now have a live Perspective table and a serializable workspace configuration. Continue with Stream data and change layouts, or run the polished complete market example.
